sections.COMMENTS:
ï»¿    **COMMENTS**
The 5 September 1950, Mw 5.7, earthquake occurred on the northern flank of the Gran Sasso range, the highest sector of the Apennines. While destructive events are numerous in inner Abruzzo (such as the 13 January 1915, Mw 7.1 one) and in the external sectors of the Apennines (like the 3 November 1706, Mw 6.8 one), this one was relatively poorly studied. Also, it suffered from a possibly incomplete intensity pattern, since the southern portion falls across the Campo Imperatore plain, an area virtually uninhabited.
However, recent studies re-assessed the macroseismic information for this somewhat poorly known earthquake (Tertulliani et al., 2006), contributing to relocating the epicenter ca. 15 km to the west. Concerning the hypocentral depth, a broad intensity field, with seemingly no damage decay away from the epicenter, suggests a deep source. Regarding the kinematics, the elongated intensity distribution along the circa E-W trending longer semi-axis suggests a source with an oblique component.
sections.OPEN QUESTIONS:
1) Is the macroseismic signature of this earthquake really conclusive about its presumed depth and kinematics?
2) What is the relationship (if any) between the causative structure of the event and the circa E-W trending northern front of the Gran Sasso range and the lineaments towards the foredeep to the east?
sections.SUMMARIES:
Di Filippo and Marcelli (1951)
They studied the 5 September 1950, Mw 5.7 earthquake. They computed epicenter and magnitude and also show the intensity distribution. The latter shows an anomalous elongation from west to east. These authors thought this event had a shallow hypocentral depth.
Scisciani et al. (2001)
They studied a transect across the Gran Sasso belt, orthogonal to the local trend of dominant contraction. They reconstructed the geometry of the thrustbelt by eliminating the effects of late folding and thrusting. The results show a major NNE-dipping extensional fault. They believe that additional NNE-dipping normal faults can be inferred from abrupt lateral variations within the siliciclastic sequences with the coarser sections systematically being found toward the northeast.
Tertulliani et al. (2006)
They carried out further studies on the macroseismic field of the 5 September 1950, augmenting the contemporary sources and hence the number of datapoints. This enabled the authors to compute a new epicentral location, further to the W, near the Campotosto Lake. They also suggest that the causative source of the 1950 earthquake could be E-W striking.
